lessons.title: HTML Document Structure
lessons.content:
Every HTML document follows a basic skeleton. The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration tells the browser this is HTML5. The <html> element is the root, <head> holds metadata like the title and links to stylesheets, and <body> holds everything the user sees.

Semantic elements like <header>, <main>, <article>, <section>, and <footer> describe the meaning of content, not just its appearance. Using them improves accessibility, SEO, and maintainability.

lessons.title: Lists & Tables
lessons.content: Ordered lists <ol> use numbers; unordered lists <ul> use bullets. Each item is an <li>. Tables use <table>, with rows <tr>, header cells <th>, and data cells <td>. Use <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> for structure.

lessons.title: Forms & Inputs
lessons.content: Forms collect user input. The <form> element wraps inputs. Each input has a type (text, email, password, number, date, checkbox, radio, etc.) and a name. Labels with for attributes link to inputs by id, improving accessibility. The <select>, <textarea>, and <button> elements round out the form toolkit.
lessons.code:
<form action="/submit" method="POST">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input type="password" id="pw" name="password" minlength="8">

  <label for="bio">Bio</label>
  <textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="4"></textarea>

  <label for="country">Country</label>
  <select id="country" name="country">
    <option value="ke">Kenya</option>
    <option value="ug">Uganda</option>
  </select>

  <button type="submit">Sign In</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Selectors & The Box Model
lessons.content: CSS selectors target HTML elements. Type selectors (p), class selectors (.btn), id selectors (#header), and attribute selectors ([type="text"]) are the basics. The box model says every element is a rectangle: content, padding, border, margin. Use box-sizing: border-box so width includes padding and border.

lessons.title: Flexbox Layouts
lessons.content: Flexbox is a 1D layout system. Set display: flex on a container; its children become flex items. Use justify-content for the main axis, align-items for the cross axis, and gap for spacing. Flex is perfect for navbars, cards, and centering things.

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.content: Grid is a 2D layout system. Define columns and rows with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows. Use the fr unit for flexible fractions. Grid is ideal for page layouts, dashboards, and galleries.

lessons.title: Animations & Transitions
lessons.content: Transitions animate between states smoothly. Animations define keyframes for more complex motion. Use transform and opacity for performance — they are GPU-accelerated. Avoid animating width, height, or top.

lessons.title: Variables, Types & Operators
lessons.content: Use let for mutable bindings, const for immutable references, and never use var. JavaScript has 7 primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint. Objects and arrays are reference types. === checks value and type; == does weird coercion — always use ===.

lessons.title: Functions, Arrows & Closures
lessons.content: Functions are first-class: they can be assigned, passed, and returned. Arrow functions don't bind their own this — perfect for callbacks. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that scope is gone.

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation & Events
lessons.content: The DOM is the live tree of HTML elements. Use querySelector and querySelectorAll to find elements. addEventListener attaches handlers. event.preventDefault() stops default actions. Use classList to toggle styles, and dataset to read data-* attributes.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript: Promises & async/await
lessons.content: JavaScript is single-threaded but non-blocking. Promises represent future values. async/await is syntactic sugar over promises that makes async code read like sync code. Always wrap await in try/catch for error handling.

lessons.title: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
lessons.content: Python uses indentation instead of braces. Variables are dynamically typed. Common types: int, float, str, bool, list, dict, tuple, set. Control flow uses if/elif/else, for, and while. List comprehensions are a Pythonic way to build lists.

lessons.title: Functions & Lambdas
lessons.content: Define functions with def. Default arguments, *args, and **kwargs give flexibility. Lambdas are anonymous one-expression functions, useful for short callbacks like sorting keys.

lessons.title: Classes & OOP
lessons.content: Classes bundle data and behavior. __init__ is the constructor. self refers to the instance. Inheritance with class Child(Parent). Use @property for getters, @classmethod and @staticmethod for class-level methods.

lessons.title: Decorators & Generators
lessons.content: Decorators wrap functions to add behavior without modifying them. Generators use yield to produce values lazily — great for large data streams. Both are cornerstone Python features.

lessons.title: Components & JSX
lessons.content: React apps are trees of components. A component is a function that returns JSX — a syntax extension that looks like HTML. Props are inputs to components. Always start component names with a capital letter.

lessons.title: State & Hooks
lessons.content: Hooks let function components use state and lifecycle. useState returns a value and setter. useEffect runs side effects — pass a dependency array to control when. Never call hooks inside loops, conditions, or nested functions.

lessons.title: Context & useReducer
lessons.content: Context shares state across many components without prop drilling. useReducer manages complex state with actions — like Redux but built-in. Combine them for a global store.

lessons.title: Data Fetching & Custom Hooks
lessons.content: Custom hooks reuse stateful logic across components. A common pattern is a useFetch hook that handles loading, error, and data. For real apps, consider React Query or SWR for caching and refetching.
